title: "The hypergeometric distribution"

The binomial distribution describes independent draws. A fixed sample drawn **without replacement** from a finite linguistic resource has less variation because each selected entry changes the composition of the remaining population. The **hypergeometric distribution** represents that design.

## A finite Turkish morphology population

We use the Turkish UniMorph release pinned at commit [6c179ac](https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b). Pimentel et al. ([2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/)) describe the morphological-reinflection task and Turkish expansion; Batsuren et al. ([2022](https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/)) describe the type-level UniMorph representation. The data are CC BY-SA 3.0.

The course population retains the distinct Turkish verb lemmas with one form in the feature cell `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL`. The pinned README says that verbs were generated semi-automatically and partially checked by a native speaker; unverified noun and adjective material is excluded. The two-character `past_suffix` is a course-derived orthographic ending, not a UniMorph morpheme boundary.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-hypergeometric
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

N <- nrow(population)
K <- sum(population$t_initial)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
x_observed <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
p_population <- K / N
finite_population_correction <- (N - n) / (N - 1)

support <- max(0L, n - (N - K)):min(n, K)
reference <- data.frame(t_initial_count = support)
reference$without_replacement <- dhyper(support, m = K, n = N - K, k = n)
reference$independent_draw <- dbinom(support, size = n, prob = p_population)

hyper_mean <- n * p_population
hyper_variance <- n * p_population * (1 - p_population) * finite_population_correction
binomial_variance <- n * p_population * (1 - p_population)

stopifnot(
  N == 588L, K == 200L, n == 120L, x_observed == 42L,
  !anyDuplicated(population$lemma),
  all(sample_120$lemma %in% population$lemma),
  abs(sum(reference$without_replacement) - 1) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(N, K, n, x_observed, hyper_mean, hyper_variance,
           binomial_variance, finite_population_correction)
```

## Mass, mean, and variance

If a population contains $N$ entries, $K$ carry a focal property, and $n$ entries are sampled without replacement, then the focal count $X$ has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)
=\frac{\binom Kx\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom Nn}.
$$

The support respects both finite stocks:

$$
\max\{0,n-(N-K)\}
\leq x\leq
\min\{n,K\}.
$$

The numerator counts samples containing $x$ focal entries and $n-x$ other entries; the denominator counts all size-$n$ samples.

Its expectation is the same as that of a binomial count with $p=K/N$, but its variance contains the **finite-population correction**:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=n\frac KN,
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=n\frac KN\left(1-\frac KN\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}.
$$

For the fixed sample, the expected number of *t*-initial endings is `r sprintf("%.3f", hyper_mean)`. The without-replacement variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", hyper_variance)`, smaller than the independent-draw variance of `r sprintf("%.3f", binomial_variance)`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-hypergeometric
#| fig-cap: "Without-replacement and independent-draw reference masses for the Turkish UniMorph sample. The vertical line marks the fixed sample count."
reference_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(count = support, probability = reference$without_replacement,
             design = "without replacement"),
  data.frame(count = support, probability = reference$independent_draw,
             design = "independent draws")
)

ggplot(reference_long, aes(count, probability, color = design, linetype = design)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x_observed, color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("without replacement" = "#8B1A1A",
                                "independent draws" = "grey45")) +
  labs(x = "t-initial forms in the fixed sample", y = "Probability",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The finite population is the pinned lexicon cell, not Turkish usage. The distribution describes repeated samples of lemmas from that resource.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute the probability of the observed count with `dhyper()`.
2. Explain why the two models have the same expectation but different variances.
3. What happens to the correction as $n/N$ approaches one?
4. Why would a corpus-token claim be unsupported by this population?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The probability of the observed count is `dhyper(42, 200, 388, 120) = 0.082787`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Both models have $\mathbb{E}[X]=nK/N=40.816327$, but sampling without replacement multiplies the binomial variance by the finite-population correction 0.797274. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. As $n/N$ approaches one, $(N-n)/(N-1)$ approaches zero and the sampling variance collapses because nearly the whole finite population is observed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The population consists of 588 distinct UniMorph verb lemmas in one feature cell, not tokens sampled from Turkish usage, so it cannot support a corpus-token claim. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
